content: The national program for preparing a country report on the elimination of onchocerciasis begins once all endemic areas have completed the post-treatment surveillance period. In Step 4, the country submits its report to the World Health Organization (WHO) through the appropriate regional office. The guidelines for stopping mass drug administration (MDA) and verifying the elimination of human onchocerciasis include conducting assessments as outlined in Annex 6, with methodologies for data collection, reporting, and analysis described in Annex 7. Based on the findings of the international verification team, the WHO Director-General issues an acknowledgment letter declaring the elimination of human onchocerciasis. Post-elimination surveillance (Phase 3) continues until the disease is eradicated across the entire region. Post-elimination surveillance involves regular assessments using O-150 PCR testing of black flies in countries where WHO has verified elimination. This continues until the risk of disease resurgence is no longer present in any country within the region. Future considerations include the potential revision of guidelines by 2020, driven by advancements in diagnostic tools, interventions, and modeling-based research on onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis. Human onchocerciasis, a vector-borne disease caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, is endemic in 31 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, three countries in Latin America, and Yemen. Chronic infection leads to severe itching, disfiguring skin lesions, and irreversible blindness. The disease is transmitted by black flies of the Simulium genus, which breed in fast-flowing rivers and streams, earning it the name river blindness. In the Americas, it is sometimes referred to as Robles’ disease after Dr. Rodolfo Robles, who first documented the link between O. volvulus and vision loss. In Africa, onchocerciasis has significant socioeconomic consequences, including the abandonment of fertile lands near vector breeding sites, which hinders economic development. Control strategies have included nodule removal (nodulectomy), vector control, and mass drug administration (MDA) with ivermectin. Ivermectin, an effective microfilaricide, temporarily reduces skin microfilarial loads to levels insufficient for transmission by black flies. It also suppresses microfilarial production in adult female worms and has a detrimental effect on adult worms, especially with repeated doses. Sustained, high-coverage MDA with ivermectin is critical for interrupting transmission and reducing morbidity. Onchocerciasis control programs using ivermectin MDA operate in three phases. Phase 1, the intervention or treatment phase, involves regular MDA with at least 80% therapeutic coverage of the eligible population. By the end of this phase, most adult worms should have died or become infertile, and transmission should be interrupted. Phase 2, post-treatment surveillance, begins when interventions are stopped. Phase 3, post-elimination surveillance, involves ongoing monitoring to confirm the absence of recrudescence. Diagnostic tests used during post-treatment surveillance must be statistically robust and include validated sample sizes of vectors and/or affected human populations. Entomological evaluations using O-150 PCR techniques assess the presence of infective-stage larvae in black flies. volvulus in children under 10 years of age. Skin snip microscopy and DEC patch tests are also used to monitor progress during treatment phases. The original WHO guidelines for certifying the elimination of onchocerciasis included criteria such as the absence of infective-stage larvae in black flies and the absence of detectable infection in untreated children or new residents in previously endemic areas. These criteria have been operationalized in Latin America and Africa, leading to the verification of elimination in Colombia (2013), Ecuador (2014), and Mexico (2015). In Africa, the shift from control to elimination programs in 2009 introduced significant operational changes and new criteria for monitoring progress. The updated guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for discontinuing MDA and verifying the elimination of O. volvulus transmission. They are intended for national onchocerciasis elimination program managers and policymakers, with the goal of adopting these recommendations as national policies. The guideline development process involved systematic reviews of the literature, expert consultations, and adherence to WHO standards for evidence assessment and recommendation formulation.
